summary: This document defines the standard format for sending mail messages between computers in the UUCP Project. It does not address how mail is stored on a machine or the lower-level transport. It sets a standard for hosts in the UUCP zone.

plainLanguage.summary: A rule for how to write down an email so one UUCP machine can pass it to the next, like how to fold a note before handing it on.

questions: what is the uucp mail format
how is mail transferred between uucp hosts
what is a hybrid address in uucp mail
subtitle: How UUCP sites wrap Internet-style mail so it can hop from machine to machine without being mangled.

tldr.problem: Mail in the UUCP world used old bang-path addresses, while the Internet used user@domain addresses. Mixing the two produced ambiguous addresses such as a!b@c.d.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 976 adopts RFC 822 for the message and RFC 920 for domains, runs the remote command rmail to move each message, and keeps the old From_ lines for the envelope.
tldr.outcome: Hosts in the UUCP zone gain one agreed format. The memo was later updated by RFC 1137, and its status is listed as Unknown in the index.

today: The index lists the status of RFC 976 as Unknown, and it was updated by RFC 1137. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Why Adopt the ARPA Standards
sections.content:
RFC 976 defines the standard format for sending mail between machines in the UUCP Project. It does not cover how a machine stores mail, or the lower-level transport. It assumes that remote execution of the rmail command (or an equivalent) is the basic operation UUCP provides.

The author's philosophy is not to invent a new standard, because that would make the UUCP world incompatible with existing systems. Instead the UUCP zone adopts RFC 822 as its mail format and RFC 920 as its domain rules. The zone is the set of UUCP-connected sites that choose to register with the UUCP project. If the ARPA community changes those standards later, the UUCP zone intends to follow, after a reasonable time to upgrade software.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making up a brand new way to write letters, the UUCP machines agree to use the same way everyone else already uses.

sections.title: Envelope, Names and Hybrid Addresses
sections.content:
A message has two parts: the envelope and the message itself. In the UUCP world the envelope is the destination addresses (the arguments to rmail) plus the source path, which sits in From or >From lines at the start of the message, called From_ lines. The RFC 822 headers such as From: and To:, and the body, are the message.

UUCP uses short host names, called 6 letter names, because every implementation treats at least the first 6 letters as significant. Domain names such as ucbvax.Berkeley.EDU are different, and are case-insensitive. A domain can be told apart from a 6 letter name because it contains at least one period.

Older UUCP software uses bang paths like a!b!c!user. A hybrid address such as a!b@c has a ! to the left of an @ and is ambiguous: it could mean (a!b)@c.d or a!(b@c.d). The RFC recommends that transport software avoid hybrid addresses and use pure bang syntax with the domain, for example c.d!a!b. A host that does accept hybrid addresses should apply the (a!b)@c.d reading, in line with RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: An address with both an exclamation mark and an at sign is like a street name that can be read two ways. The RFC says to avoid writing it that way.

sections.title: Transport with rmail and Batch SMTP
sections.content:
Because SMTP is not available to much of the UUCP domain, the RFC defines the command run on the remote machine: rmail user@domain ..., with the message on standard input. More than one address is allowed, to save transmission cost when a message has several recipients. An alternative form is rmail domain!user, where the domain contains at least one period and no !; it means exactly the same thing and survives old UUCP hosts that might rewrite an address. Routing through old hosts can look like rmail a!b!c!domain!user. A single-level domain gets a trailing period, as in att.!Mark.Horton.

The user part may contain any character except @, and the % character should be avoided because some hosts treat it as a synonym for @.

Implementations may also support Batch SMTP, which is a series of SMTP commands (see RFC 821) sent in one file for batch execution. Mail to the user b-smtp is read as these commands. Each line gets an extra hash character at the start so that a lone period does not look like an end-of-file marker. The benefit is that the Unix shell does not interpret the message, so characters such as spaces and parentheses are safe.
sections.plainLanguage: Each machine runs a little mail command on the next one and hands over the letter. You can also pack many instructions in one parcel and let the other end unpack them.

sections.title: The Envelope and From_ Lines
sections.content:
The standard input of rmail begins with a single line of the form From domain!user date remote from system, followed straight away by the RFC 822 headers and body. More From_ lines may precede it, one added by each system the message passes through, and the system names may be stacked into one line with many ! characters. A > may precede the word From.

The main change from earlier UUCP mail is that the stacked path now includes the domain, for example a!b!c!mysys!domain!me rather than a!b!c!mysys!me. If the domain! part is redundant it may be omitted.

A receiving system may merge several From_ lines into one. Adding a Received line from this information is discouraged, because it would look as if a different system had added it; a Sent-By line is the safer choice. When a system stores the message in a local mailbox it should generate a single From_ line, keeping the date format. If an intermediate system adds text such as system! in front of a user@domain address, that violates both this standard and RFC 822.
sections.plainLanguage: Every machine that passes the letter along stamps its name on the outside, so you can see the path it took.

sections.title: Host Classes and the Routing Algorithm
sections.content:
To route mail well, a sender sometimes needs to know what software the next host runs. The RFC sorts hosts into three classes. Class 1 understands only old-style bang routing, such as rmail user and rmail host1!host2!user, and is the safe assumption for an unknown host. Class 2 adds 4.2BSD-style domain parsing, so it understands rmail user@domain for domains it knows. Class 3 has all of that, can route mail for hosts that are not adjacent, and understands rmail domain!user. All gateways into UUCP must be class 3, and this document describes what class 3 hosts must handle.

The delivery algorithm for user@domain has these steps:

  • If the address has the form @domain1:user@domain2, use domain1 as the domain.
  • Find the most specific part of the domain recognized locally in a routing table, searched from specific to general.
  • Read the gateway g and the UUCP route r from the table entry.
  • Take the first hop of r as the next hop n, which is always directly connected.
  • Work out the class of g and n if possible, build a destination string, and pass the message to n.

If the next hop is not known to be class 3, the ! form should be used if possible, since a hybrid address is hard to predict. Hosts that exchange significant traffic are expected to set up a direct UUCP link and add a table entry for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some machines are clever and some are old. You look in a list to find the next machine to hand the letter to, and you write the address in the way that machine can understand.

sections.title: What Conforming Hosts Must Accept
sections.content:
Hosts that conform to this standard should accept all of these forms: rmail localuser, rmail hosta!hostb!user, rmail user@domain, rmail domain!user and rmail domain.!user (for a domain with no dots).

The envelope (the From_ lines) follows existing conventions with ! routing. The header lines such as Date:, From:, To: and Subject: must conform to RFC 822, and all header addresses must be in the @ form. The originating site is responsible for legal addresses. Forwarding sites and gateways should NOT turn a legal RFC 822 address such as user@domain into an illegal one such as gateway!user@domain, even when forwarding to a class 1 host. The memo does not have a separate security section.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules boil down to this: write the outside label the old way, write the letter inside the new way, and never scribble on someone else's address.

items.label: Old-style ! routing only
items.desc: Understands rmail user and rmail host1!host2!user; assume nothing more.

items.label: Bang paths plus domain parsing
items.desc: Also understands rmail user@domain for domains it knows.

items.label: Full support
items.desc: Also routes for non-adjacent hosts and understands rmail domain!user.
